claim: DeepLabCut is a state-of-the-art animal pose estimation package that provides tailored networks to predict the posture of animals based on video frames.
source: One such state-of-the-art animal pose estimation package, DeepLabCut (DLC; Mathis et al., 2018b), provides tailored networks that predict the posture of animals of interest based on video frames, and can run swiftly in offline batch processing modes (up to 2500 FPS on standard GPUs; Mathis et al., 2020a; Mathis and Warren, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Mathis et al., 2018b; Mathis et al., 2020a; Mathis and Warren, 2018) describing DeepLabCut's capabilities.

claim: DeepLabCut can run at up to 2500 FPS on standard GPUs in offline batch processing modes.
source: One such state-of-the-art animal pose estimation package, DeepLabCut (DLC; Mathis et al., 2018b), provides tailored networks that predict the posture of animals of interest based on video frames, and can run swiftly in offline batch processing modes (up to 2500 FPS on standard GPUs; Mathis et al., 2020a; Mathis and Warren, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Mathis et al., 2020a; Mathis and Warren, 2018) documenting DeepLabCut's processing speeds.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package achieves low-latency real-time pose estimation within 15 ms at over 100 FPS.
source: Here, we provide a new DeepLabCut-Live! package that achieves low-latency real-time pose estimation (within 15 ms, >100 FPS), with an additional forward-prediction module that achieves zero-latency feedback, and a dynamic-cropping mode that allows for higher inference speeds.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing latency and frame rate measurements.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package includes a forward-prediction module that achieves zero-latency feedback.
source: Here, we provide a new DeepLabCut-Live! package that achieves low-latency real-time pose estimation (within 15 ms, >100 FPS), with an additional forward-prediction module that achieves zero-latency feedback, and a dynamic-cropping mode that allows for higher inference speeds.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the forward-prediction module's performance in achieving sub-zero latency.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package includes a dynamic-cropping mode that allows for higher inference speeds.
source: Here, we provide a new DeepLabCut-Live! package that achieves low-latency real-time pose estimation (within 15 ms, >100 FPS), with an additional forward-prediction module that achieves zero-latency feedback, and a dynamic-cropping mode that allows for higher inference speeds.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing inference speed improvements with dynamic cropping.

claim: Three options are provided for using DeepLabCut-Live!: a stand-alone GUI (DLC-Live! GUI), integration into Bonsai, and integration into AutoPilot.
source: We also provide three options for using this tool with ease: (1) a stand-alone GUI (called DLC-Live! GUI), and integration into (2) Bonsai, and (3) AutoPilot.
evidence: The claim is supported by descriptions and experimental demonstrations of each interface throughout the manuscript.

claim: Performance was benchmarked on a wide range of systems including different GPUs, CPUs, and operating systems.
source: Lastly, we benchmarked performance on a wide range of systems so that experimentalists can easily decide what hardware is required for their needs.
evidence: The claim is supported by extensive benchmarking data presented in tables and figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Existing real-time pose estimation software has slower speed and higher latency than the DeepLabCut-Live! package.
source: First, we provide a marked speed and latency improvement from existing real-time pose estimation software (Forys et al., 2020; Štih et al., 2019; Schweihoff et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to existing software and comparative performance data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package optimizes inference code and uses lightweight DeepLabCut models that perform well on GPUs, CPUs, and affordable embedded systems such as the NVIDIA Jetson platform.
source: Although these tools are also built on top of DeepLabCut, our software optimizes inference code and uses lightweight DeepLabCut models that perform well not only on GPUs, but also on CPUs and affordable embedded systems such as the NVIDIA Jetson platform.
evidence: The claim is supported by benchmarking data showing performance across different hardware platforms including Jetson systems.

claim: A module was introduced to export trained neural network models and load them into other platforms with ease.
source: Second, we introduce a module to export trained neural network models and load them into other platforms with ease, improving the ability to transfer trained models between machines, to share trained models with other users, and to load trained models in other software packages.
evidence: The claim is supported by descriptions of the model export functionality and its implementation in the manuscript.

claim: Easy loading of trained models into other software packages enabled integration of DeepLabCut into Bonsai.
source: Easy loading of trained models into other software packages enabled integration of DeepLabCut into another popular systems neuroscience software, Bonsai (Lopes et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description and demonstration of the Bonsai-DLC plugin in the manuscript.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package has minimal software dependencies and can easily be installed on integrated systems such as the NVIDIA Jetson platform.
source: Third, we provide a new lightweight DeepLabCut-Live! package to run DeepLabCut inference online (or offline). This package has minimal software dependencies and can easily be installed on integrated systems, such as the NVIDIA Jetson platform.
evidence: The claim is supported by descriptions of the package design and demonstrations of its use on Jetson systems.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package is designed to enable easy integration of real-time pose estimation into custom software applications.
source: Furthermore, it is designed to enable easy integration of real-time pose estimation using DeepLabCut into custom software applications.
evidence: The claim is supported by demonstrations of integration into AutoPilot and descriptions of the SDK design.

claim: Integration of DeepLabCut-Live! into the AutoPilot framework demonstrates the ability to integrate real-time pose estimation into custom software applications.
source: We demonstrate this ability via integration of DeepLabCut-Live! into the new AutoPilot framework (Saunders and Wehr, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental demonstrations of the AutoPilot integration presented in the manuscript.

claim: Low latency real-time pose estimation was achieved with delays as low as 10 ms using GPUs.
source: Using these new software tools, we achieve low latency real-time pose estimation, with delays as low as 10 ms using GPUs and 30 ms using CPUs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing latency measurements on GPU systems.

claim: Low latency real-time pose estimation was achieved with delays as low as 30 ms using CPUs.
source: Using these new software tools, we achieve low latency real-time pose estimation, with delays as low as 10 ms using GPUs and 30 ms using CPUs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing latency measurements on CPU systems.

claim: The forward-prediction module enables ultra-low latency feedback to an animal, even down to sub-zero ms delay.
source: Furthermore, we introduce a forward-prediction module that counteracts these delays by predicting the animal's future pose. Using this forward-prediction module, we were able to provide ultra-low latency feedback to an animal (even down to sub-zero ms delay).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the dog feedback experiment showing negative latencies.

claim: Such short latencies have only been approachable in marked animals but have not been achieved previously with markerless pose estimation.
source: Such short latencies have only been approachable in marked animals (Sehara et al., 2019), but have not been achieved to the best of our knowledge previously with markerless pose estimation (Zhao et al., 2019; Forys et al., 2020; Štih et al., 2019; Schweihoff et al., 2019; Privitera et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on marked and markerless tracking systems.

claim: A benchmarking suite was developed to test the performance of these tools on multiple hardware and software platforms.
source: Lastly, we developed a benchmarking suite to test the performance of these tools on multiple hardware and software platforms.
evidence: The claim is supported by descriptions of the benchmarking methodology and presentation of results.

claim: Performance metrics were provided for ten different GPUs, two integrated systems, and five CPUs across different operating systems.
source: We provide performance metrics for ten different GPUs, two integrated systems and five CPUs across different operation systems.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comprehensive benchmarking data presented in tables and figures.

claim: The benchmarking suite is openly shared at https://github.com/DeepLabCut/DeepLabCut-live.
source: We openly share this benchmarking suite at https://github.com/DeepLabCut/DeepLabCut-live; Kane, 2020; copy archived at swh:1:rev:02cd95312ec6673414bdc4ca4c8d9b6c263e7e2f so that users can look up expected inference speeds and run the benchmark on their system.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with a URL and archive reference.

claim: The model export module utilizes the protocol buffer format (.pb file).
source: The model export module utilizes the protocol buffer format (.pb file).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section describing the export functionality.

claim: Protocol buffers are a language-neutral, platform-neutral extensible mechanism for serializing structured data.
source: Protocol buffers are a language-neutral, platform-neutral extensible mechanism for serializing structured data (https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers), which makes sharing models simple.
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to the protocol buffers documentation.

claim: Sharing a whole DeepLabCut project is not necessary when using the protocol buffer format; an end-user can simply point to the protocol buffer file of a model to run inference on novel videos.
source: Sharing a whole (DeepLabCut) project is not necessary, and an end-user can simply point to the protocol buffer file of a model to run inference on novel videos (online or offline).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a feature of the protocol buffer export functionality.

claim: The flexibility offered by the protocol buffer format allowed integration of DeepLabCut into applications written in different languages including a new python package DeepLabCut-Live! and Bonsai written in C#.
source: The flexibility offered by the protocol buffer format allowed us to integrate DeepLabCut into applications written in different languages: a new python package DeepLabCut-Live!, which facilitates loading DeepLabCut networks to run inference; and into Bonsai, which is written in C# and runs DeepLabCut inference using TensorFlowSharp (https://github.com/migueldeicaza/TensorFlowSharp).
evidence: The claim is supported by descriptions of the implementations in Python and C#.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package provides a simple programming interface to load exported DeepLabCut models and perform pose estimation on single images.
source: The DeepLabCut-Live! package provides a simple programming interface to load exported DeepLabCut models and perform pose estimation on single images (i.e., from a camera feed).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the package functionality.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package has minimal dependencies and can be easily installed even on integrated systems.
source: By design, this package has minimal dependencies and can be easily installed even on integrated systems.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a design feature of the package.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package uses a Processor class to provide closed-loop feedback based on poses estimated by DeepLabCut.
source: To use poses estimated by DeepLabCut to provide closed-loop feedback, the DeepLabCut-Live! package uses a Processor class.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the package architecture.

claim: A Processor class must contain two methods: process and save.
source: A Processor class must contain two methods: process and save.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a requirement for the Processor class.

claim: The process method takes a pose as an argument, performs some operation such as giving a command to control external hardware, and returns a processed pose.
source: The process method takes a pose as an argument, performs some operation, such as giving a command to control external hardware (e.g. to give reward or to turn on a laser for optogenetic stimulation), and returns a processed pose.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the process method.

claim: The save method allows the user to save data recorded by the Processor in any format the user desires.
source: The save method allows the user to save data recorded by the Processor in any format the user desires.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the save method.

claim: The Processor object can be used to read and write from a variety of commonly used data acquisition and input/output devices including National Instruments devices, Arduino and Teensy micro-controllers, Raspberry Pis and similar embedded systems.
source: By imposing few constraints on the Processor object, this tool is very flexible; for example, it can be used to read and write from a variety of commonly used data acquisition and input/output devices, including National Instruments devices, Arduino and Teensy micro-controllers, as well as Raspberry Pis and similar embedded systems.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a feature of the Processor flexibility.

claim: An example Processor object that uses a Teensy micro-controller to control a laser for optogenetics is provided in the DeepLabCut-Live! package.
source: An example Processor object that uses a Teensy micro-controller to control a laser for optogenetics is provided in the DeepLabCut-Live! package.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an example provided with the package.

claim: Factors that influence inference speed of DeepLabCut networks include the size of the network, the size of images, and the computational power of the hardware.
source: Some known factors that influence inference speed of DeepLabCut networks include (i) the size of the network (Mathis et al., 2020b; Mathis et al., 2020a), (ii) the size of images (Mathis and Warren, 2018), and (iii) the computational power of the hardware (Mathis and Warren, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work documenting these factors.

claim: The DeepLabCut-Live! package offers three methods to increase inference speed by reducing the size of images: static image cropping, dynamic cropping around keypoints, and downsizing images.
source: The DeepLabCut-Live! package offers three convenient methods to increase inference speed by reducing the size of images: static image cropping, dynamic cropping around keypoints, and downsizing images (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental demonstrations in the manuscript.

claim: Inference speeds were faster for the smaller DLC-MobileNetV2-0.35 networks than the larger DLC-ResNet-50v1 networks.
source: As expected, inference speeds were faster for the smaller DLC-MobileNetV2-0.35 networks than the larger DLC-ResNet-50v1 networks (Mathis et al., 2020a), faster with smaller images, and faster when using more powerful NVIDIA GPUs compared to smaller GPUs or CPUs (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2 and cited prior work.

claim: Inference speeds were faster with smaller images.
source: As expected, inference speeds were faster for the smaller DLC-MobileNetV2-0.35 networks than the larger DLC-ResNet-50v1 networks (Mathis et al., 2020a), faster with smaller images, and faster when using more powerful NVIDIA GPUs compared to smaller GPUs or CPUs (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Inference speeds were faster when using more powerful NVIDIA GPUs compared to smaller GPUs or CPUs.
source: As expected, inference speeds were faster for the smaller DLC-MobileNetV2-0.35 networks than the larger DLC-ResNet-50v1 networks (Mathis et al., 2020a), faster with smaller images, and faster when using more powerful NVIDIA GPUs compared to smaller GPUs or CPUs (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: With the NVIDIA Titan RTX GPU (24 GB), inference speeds of 152 ± 15 frames per second were achieved on medium sized images (459 × 349 pixels) using the MobileNetV2-0.35 DeepLabCut network.
source: For example, with the NVIDIA Titan RTX GPU (24 GB) and the NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 GPU (8 GB), we achieved inference speeds of 152 ± 15 and 134 ± 9 frames per second on medium sized images (459 × 349 pixels) using the MobileNetV2-0.35 DeepLabCut network.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from benchmarking tests.

claim: With the NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 GPU (8 GB), inference speeds of 134 ± 9 frames per second were achieved on medium sized images (459 × 349 pixels) using the MobileNetV2-0.35 DeepLabCut network.
source: For example, with the NVIDIA Titan RTX GPU (24 GB) and the NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 GPU (8 GB), we achieved inference speeds of 152 ± 15 and 134 ± 9 frames per second on medium sized images (459 × 349 pixels) using the MobileNetV2-0.35 DeepLabCut network.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from benchmarking tests.

claim: The best accuracy was achieved on the largest images using networks trained on large images (RMSE = 2.90 pixels at image scale = 150% and training scales of 50–125% or 10–125%).
source: Naturally, the best accuracy was achieved on the largest images using networks trained on large images (RMSE = 2.90 pixels at image scale = 150% and training scales of 50–125% or 10–125%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from accuracy testing on different image scales.

claim: There was only minimal loss in accuracy when downsizing images to a scale of 25% of the image size.
source: However, there was only minimal loss in accuracy when downsizing images to a scale of 25% of the image size, and these errors were mitigated by using a network trained specifically on smaller images (RMSE = 7.59 pixels at 25% scale with training scale = 10–50%; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For the smallest images tested (test scale = 12.5%), accuracy suffered on all networks (RMSE = 26.99–70.92).
source: However, for the smallest images tested (test scale = 12.5%), accuracy suffered on all networks (RMSE = 26.99–70.92; all RMSE reported as would be in the original image (640 × 480) for comparability), likely because the mouse is only about 10 pixels long.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from accuracy testing on very small images.

claim: Dynamic cropping can provide a speed boost.
source: Another alternative is to not to downsize, but rather to process only the portion of the image that contains the animal. Our approach, which we call 'dynamic cropping', can provide a speed boost (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dynamic cropping increased inference speed by 75% (full image: 59.6 ± 2.08; dynamic-50: 103.7 ± 19.8; dynamic-25: 110.8 ± 17.6; dynamic-10: 108 ± 25.2).
source: Dynamic cropping increased inference speed by 75% (full image: 59.6 ± 2.08; dynamic-50: 103.7 ± 19.8; dynamic-25: 110.8 ± 17.6; dynamic-10: 108 ± 25.2; mean ± standard deviation), and resulted in only a small change in tracking performance, with RMSEs of 4.4, 5.5, and 20.6 for dynamic cropping with 50, 25, and 10 pixel margins, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic cropping tests.

claim: Dynamic cropping resulted in only a small change in tracking performance, with RMSEs of 4.4, 5.5, and 20.6 for dynamic cropping with 50, 25, and 10 pixel margins, respectively.
source: Dynamic cropping increased inference speed by 75% (full image: 59.6 ± 2.08; dynamic-50: 103.7 ± 19.8; dynamic-25: 110.8 ± 17.6; dynamic-10: 108 ± 25.2; mean ± standard deviation), and resulted in only a small change in tracking performance, with RMSEs of 4.4, 5.5, and 20.6 for dynamic cropping with 50, 25, and 10 pixel margins, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic cropping accuracy tests.

claim: The number of keypoints in the model had no effect on inference speed.
source: The number of keypoints in the model had no effect on inference speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The DLC-Live! GUI provides a graphical user interface that simultaneously controls capturing data from a camera, recording videos, and performing pose estimation and closed-loop feedback using the DeepLabCut-Live! package.
source: The DLG provides a graphical user interface that simultaneously controls capturing data from a camera (many camera types are supported, see Materials and methods), recording videos, and performing pose estimation and closed-loop feedback using the DeepLabCut-Live! package.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the DLG functionality.

claim: Video data acquisition and pose estimation run in parallel in the DLC-Live! GUI to allow users to both record video and perform pose estimation at the fastest possible rates.
source: To allow users to both record video and perform pose estimation at the fastest possible rates, these processes run in parallel.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a design feature of the DLG.

claim: DLG offers users a choice between 'Optimize Rate' mode and 'Optimize Latency' mode.
source: DLG offers users a choice of which mode they prefer: an 'Optimize Rate' mode, in which pose estimation is performed at the maximum possible rate, but there may be delays from the time an image was captured to the time pose estimation begins, and an 'Optimize Latency' mode, in which the pose estimation process waits for a new image to be acquired, minimizing the delay from the time an image was acquired to when the pose becomes available.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of DLG modes.

claim: On a Windows system with GeForce GTX 1080 GPU, DLG achieved delays from frame acquisition to obtaining the pose as fast as 10 ± 1 ms in the 'Optimize Latency' mode.
source: On a Windows system with GeForce GTX 1080 GPU, DLG achieved delays from frame acquisition to obtaining the pose as fast as 10 ± 1 ms (mean ± sd) in the 'Optimize Latency' mode.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DLG performance testing.

claim: The delay from acquiring an image in which the tongue was detected until the LED could be turned on/off includes the time needed to obtain the pose, plus additional time to determine if the tongue is present and to execute the control signal.
source: Lastly, the delay from acquiring an image in which the tongue was detected until the LED could turned on/off includes the time needed to obtain the pose, plus additional time to determine if the tongue is present and to execute the control signal (send a TTL pulse to the LED).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the latency measurement methodology.

claim: Detecting the tongue and sending a TTL pulse only took an additional 0.4 ms (95% CI: 0.3–0.6 ms).
source: Detecting the tongue and sending a TTL pulse only took an additional 0.4 ms (95% CI: 0.3–0.6 ms).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse licking feedback experiment.

claim: Bonsai is a widely used visual language for reactive programming, real-time behavior tracking, synchronization of multiple data streams and closed-loop experiments.
source: Bonsai is a widely used visual language for reactive programming, real-time behavior tracking, synchronization of multiple data streams and closed-loop experiments (Lopes et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Bonsai publication.

claim: A Bonsai-DLC plugin was developed that allows loading of DeepLabCut exported .pb files directly in Bonsai.
source: We developed equivalent performance benchmarks for testing our newly developed Bonsai-DLC plugin https://github.com/bonsai-rx/deeplabcut. This plugin allows loading of the DeepLabCut exported .pb files directly in Bonsai.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the Bonsai integration.

claim: The performance of running inference through Bonsai-DLC was comparable to DeepLabCut-Live! inference.
source: We compared the performance of Bonsai-DLC and DeepLabCut-Live! on a Windows 10 computer with GeForce GTX 1080 with Max-Q design GPU and found that the performance of running inference through Bonsai-DLC was comparable to DeepLabCut-Live! inference (Figure 4), suggesting that, as expected, inference speed is limited primarily by available CPU/GPU computational resources rather than by any native language interface optimizations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing Bonsai-DLC and DeepLabCut-Live! performance.

claim: The latency using Bonsai-DLC was 34 ms ± 9.5 ms (median, IQR, n = 500) tested at 30 Hz with 384 × 307 pixels.
source: Moreover, we found the latency to be 34 ms ± 9.5 ms (median, IQR, n = 500) tested at 30 Hz with 384 × 307 pixels, which is equivalent to what was found with DLG above.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Bonsai-DLC latency testing.

claim: As the number of particle interactions increased the GPU load, there was a corresponding drop in DLC inference speeds.
source: Overall, we found that as the number of particle interactions increased the GPU load, there was a corresponding drop in DLC inference speeds (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GPU load testing with particle simulations.

claim: As long as GPU load remained balanced, there was no obvious effect on inference speeds, suggesting that in many cases, it would be possible to combine closed-loop accelerated DeepLabCut-live inference with real-time visual environments running on the same GPU.
source: Nevertheless, as long as GPU load remained balanced, there was no obvious effect on inference speeds, suggesting that in many cases, it would be possible to combine closed-loop accelerated DeepLabCut-live inference with real-time visual environments running on the same GPU (Lopes et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GPU load testing and cited work on visual environments.

claim: Autopilot is a Python framework designed to overcome problems of simultaneously collecting multiple streams of data by distributing different data streams over a swarm of networked computers.
source: Autopilot is a Python framework designed to overcome problems of simultaneously collecting multiple streams of data by distributing different data streams over a swarm of networked computers (Saunders and Wehr, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Autopilot publication.

claim: DeepLabCut-Live! was integrated into Autopilot in a new module of composable data transformation objects.
source: Thus, we integrated DeepLabCut-Live! into Autopilot in a new module of composable data transformation objects.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the Autopilot integration.

claim: Frame rate had little effect on latency with smaller images, but at 512 × 416, latencies at 30 FPS (median = 161.3 ms) were 38.6 and 52.6 ms longer than at 60 FPS (median = 122.7 ms) and 90 FPS (median = 113.7 ms), respectively.
source: Frame rate had a little effect with smaller images, but at 512 × 416, latencies at 30 FPS (median = 161.3 ms, IQR = [145.6–164.4], n = 500) were 38.6 and 52.6 ms longer than at 60 FPS (median = 122.7 ms, IQR = [109.4–159.3], n = 500) and 90 FPS (median = 113.7 ms, IQR = [106.7–118.5], n = 500), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Autopilot latency testing at different frame rates.

claim: With smaller images (128 × 128 and 256 × 256), inference time was the source of roughly half of the total latency.
source: WIth smaller images (128 × 128 and 256 × 256), inference time (shaded areas in Figure 5B) was the source of roughly half of the total latency (inference/median total latency, n = 1500 each, pooled across frame rates. 128 × 128: 32.2/64.6 ms = 49.7%. 256 x 256: 34.5/65.1 ms = 53.0%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Autopilot latency analysis.

claim: At 512 × 416, inference time accounted for between 50% and 70% of total latency.
source: At 512 × 416, inference time accounted for between 50% and 70% of total latency (512 × 416, 30 FPS: 79.9/161.3ms = 49.5%, 90 FPS: 79.9/113.7 ms = 70.3%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Autopilot latency analysis.

claim: DeepLabCut-Live! in Autopilot is very usable with $350 of computing power (TX2 and Raspberry Pi 4).
source: Minimizing instrument cost for experimental reproducibility and scientific equity is a primary design principle of Autopilot, so while noting that it would be trivial to reduce latency by using a faster GPU or the lower-latency Jetson Xavier (i.e. see above sections), we emphasize that DeepLabCut-Live! in Autopilot is very usable with $350 of computing power (TX2 with education discount: $299, Jetson TX2 with NVIDIA Exclusive Education Discount: https://web.archive.org/web/20200723081533/; https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/jetson-tx2-education-discount/; Raspberry Pi 4 2 GB RAM: $35, Raspberry Pi from Adafruit: https://web.archive.org/web/20200426114340/; https://www.adafruit.com/product/4292).
evidence: The claim is supported by cost information and performance data from the Autopilot experiments.

claim: Autopilot has approximately 25 ms of overhead (median of latency - mean DeepLabCut inference time - 1/2 inter-frame interval = 25.4 ms, IQR = [14.7–37.9], n = 4500).
source: Subtracting latency that is intrinsic to the experiment (frame acquisition asynchrony and GPU speed), Autopilot has approximately 25 ms of overhead (median of latency - mean DeepLabCut inference time - 1/2 inter-frame interval = 25.4 ms, IQR = [14.7–37.9], n = 4500).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Autopilot latency analysis.

claim: A DeepLabCut network based on the ResNet-50 architecture was trained to track 20 keypoints on the face, body, forelimbs, and hindlimbs of a dog.
source: First, a DeepLabCut network based on the ResNet-50 architecture (DLC-ResNet-50v1) was trained to track 20 keypoints on the face, body, forelimbs, and hindlimbs of a dog (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the dog feedback experiment.

claim: The Jetson Xavier running DLG was used to record the dog as she performed a series of 'rearing' movements in response to verbal commands, with treats given periodically by an experimenter.
source: Next, the Jetson Xavier running DLG was used to record the dog as she performed a series of 'rearing' movements in response to verbal commands, with treats given periodically by an experimenter.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the dog feedback experiment.

claim: The dog was considered to be in a 'rearing' posture if the vertical position of at least one of the elbows was above the vertical position of the withers.
source: The dog was considered to be in a 'rearing' posture if the vertical position of at least one of the elbows was above the vertical position of the withers (between the shoulder blades).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the description of the rearing detection algorithm.

claim: The dog feedback setup achieved a rate of pose estimation of 22.417 ± 0.928 frames per second, with an image to pose latency of 61 ± 10 ms (N = 1848 frames).
source: This setup achieved a rate of pose estimation of 22.417 ± 0.928 frames per second, with an image to pose latency of 61 ± 10 ms (N = 1848 frames) and, on images for which the LED was turned on or off, an image to LED latency of 59 ± 11 ms (N = 9 'rearing' movements).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the dog feedback experiment.

claim: On images for which the LED was turned on or off, there was an image to LED latency of 59 ± 11 ms (N = 9 'rearing' movements).
source: This setup achieved a rate of pose estimation of 22.417 ± 0.928 frames per second, with an image to pose latency of 61 ± 10 ms (N = 1848 frames) and, on images for which the LED was turned on or off, an image to LED latency of 59 ± 11 ms (N = 9 'rearing' movements).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the dog feedback experiment.

claim: According to offline analysis of all recorded frames, there was a delay of 70 ± 23 ms to turn the LED on or off.
source: According to this analysis, there was a delay of 70 ± 23 ms to turn the LED on or off (consistent with estimates on Jetson systems shown above, see Figure 3).

claim: A Kalman filter was implemented that estimated the position, velocity, and acceleration of each keypoint, and used this information to predict the position of each keypoint at the current point in time.
